title: Review: The heart and cardiac cycle; Dissection and tissue studies; Cardiovascular disease and risk
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX07#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR05a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX07#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR05a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX07#N.6, EX13a#N.11a, EX13b#N.3, PR05b#N.11, EX07#N.3, EX13a#N.5, EX13b#N.6, EX07#N.14, EX13b#N.11, EX13b#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Septum
items.clue: Wall that keeps the two sides of the heart apart and stops blood mixing

items.label: Magnification
items.clue: Size of the drawing divided by the actual size, both in the same units.

items.label: Diastole
items.clue: About 0.4 s in which all chambers relax and blood flows in from the veins

items.label: Annotation
items.clue: A label plus a short note on what a structure does or a feature you can see.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node fires. Which sequence of events then follows in the left side of the heart?

options.text: The atrium and the ventricle contract at the same moment, and the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open together to let blood into the aorta.
The atrium contracts, filling the ventricle; the ventricle then contracts, shutting the atrioventricular valve and opening the semilunar valve; then both relax.
Muscles attached to the valves pull them open one after the other, and the ventricle contracts only after both valves have been opened.
A nerve impulse from the brain reaches the ventricle first, so the ventricle contracts and then the atrium contracts to refill it.

questions.explanation: Atrial systole completes ventricular filling. The ventricle's rising pressure shuts the AV valve and, once above aortic pressure, opens the semilunar valve. Diastole follows.

questions.stem: A man has atheroma in a carotid artery, which carries blood to the brain. A plaque ruptures. What is most likely to happen next?

options.text: Fat from his blood keeps sticking to the exposed plaque until, over a few hours, the carotid artery bursts open.
The ruptured plaque stops blood passing through the chambers of his heart, so no blood reaches his brain.
The smooth muscle of the artery wall contracts to push the broken plaque along the vessel to his brain.
A clot forms at the rupture and blocks this artery or a smaller one; brain tissue beyond lacks oxygen.

questions.explanation: Same chain as a heart attack: damaged wall → plaque → rupture → clot → occlusion. In the brain, the result is a stroke.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. In a study of 20 countries, the correlation coefficient between mean saturated fat intake and the death rate from coronary heart disease was +0.85. What can be concluded from this result alone?

options.text: There is a strong positive correlation between the variables, but this does not prove that one causes the other.
Saturated fat in the diet is shown to cause coronary heart disease, because the coefficient is so close to +1, the maximum.
The relationship is weak, because a correlation calculated from only 20 countries cannot be a strong one.
Saturated fat from food coats the inside of the coronary arteries, which is why the two variables rise together in step.

questions.stem: A student dissects a set of sheep's lungs. Near the lungs she finds two tubes side by side. Tube P has C-shaped rings of cartilage in its wall and stays open when empty. Tube Q has a thin, soft wall with no cartilage and collapses flat. Which identification do these observations best support?

options.text: P is an artery: it has the thicker wall and stays open, as arteries do.
P is a bronchus, held open by its cartilage; Q is a blood vessel.
Q is an artery: blood at high pressure needs a wide, soft-walled vessel.
Q is a vein, because it carries blood that is low in oxygen.

questions.explanation: Structure identifies it: C-shaped cartilage keeps airways open. A thin wall that collapses fits a vein, such as a pulmonary vein.

questions.stem: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Which statement correctly explains this difference?

options.text: The left ventricle pumps a larger volume of blood at each beat than the right ventricle, so it needs more muscle.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which offer more resistance to flow than the rest of the body does.
The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circulation.
The left ventricle gets a stronger nerve impulse from the brain at each beat, so it has built up more muscle.

questions.stem: A blood clot completely occludes a branch of a coronary artery. What is the direct consequence?

options.text: Blood can no longer pass through the chambers of the heart, so the heart stops beating almost at once.
The region of cardiac muscle supplied by that branch is deprived of oxygen and its cells die.
Fat from the diet keeps building up on the surface of the clot until the artery bursts open.
The muscle in the artery wall contracts to force the clot along, tearing the artery wall.

questions.explanation: The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.

questions.stem: Early epidemiological studies found that women taking HRT had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD). Later randomised controlled trials found that HRT slightly increased CHD risk. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The early studies were correct because they involved far more women than the trials did, so their result should be preferred.
The correlation was not causal: women on HRT tended to have higher socioeconomic status, which itself lowers CHD risk.
HRT must lower CHD risk in most women, and the trials must have happened to sample an unusual group of women.
The early correlation must have been a chance result: women on HRT did not really have lower CHD rates.

questions.stem: Pressures in the right side of a heart, early in ventricular systole: right atrium 0.4 kPa; right ventricle 1.0 kPa and rising; pulmonary artery 1.3 kPa. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The atrioventricular valve is open, because pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the atrium.
The semilunar valve is open, because the ventricle is contracting.
Both valves will open when the pacemaker sends a nerve signal to them.
Both valves are shut; the semilunar valve will open once ventricular pressure exceeds 1.3 kPa.

questions.explanation: Ventricle above atrium shuts the AV valve; ventricle below artery keeps the semilunar valve shut. As pressure keeps rising, it opens.

questions.stem: A woman has a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.65 m. What is her BMI?

options.text: 25.7 kg m⁻²
21.2 kg m⁻²
42.4 kg m⁻²

questions.stem: Illustrative data. A study of 2000 adults found a correlation coefficient of −0.40 between hours of golf played per week and the incidence of coronary heart disease. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Playing golf probably protects against coronary heart disease, since the correlation shows that more golf goes with less disease.
There is almost no relationship, because a negative coefficient always shows a weak link between two variables.
The relationship must be strong, since it was measured in 2000 people and sample size shows how strong a link is.
More golf goes with less disease, moderately; a confounder such as income may explain it, so cause is not shown.
